title: US arms-transfer dominance can deepen allied dependence without proving political control
source_unit: SIPRI Arms Transfers Database and Trends in International Arms Transfers 2025 fact sheet
geography: International transfers of major conventional arms; United States, Europe, and European NATO members

denominator.unit: SIPRI volume of transfers of major conventional arms between states

us_export_share_prior_period.unit: percent of global major-arms exports in 2016-2020

observations.method: SIPRI five-year comparison using the Arms Transfers Database; transfer volume is measured in SIPRI's TIV-based framework rather than financial value.
observations.uncertainty: Five-year transfer volumes smooth timing but do not identify order, delivery, training, maintenance, operational use, political consent, or strategic effect; secrecy and data limitations affect some cases.
observations.subgroup: States, suppliers, recipient regions, Europe, and European NATO members receiving major conventional arms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Import growth can reflect threat perception, aid, replacement, timing, or a few large systems; concentration can coexist with recipient diversification, domestic production, or political resistance.

related_sources.claim: SIPRI's 2025 fact sheet reports supplier shares, recipient regions, and the US-European transfer relationship.
SIPRI describes the updated 1950-2025 Arms Transfers Database and its transfer-volume and supplier-recipient uses.

boundary: This record measures international major-arms transfer volumes and supplier concentration. It does not establish financial value, delivery, operational readiness, sustainment, recipient autonomy, public consent, alliance obedience, deterrence, or strategic leverage.
